title: Latency-conscious tool adaptor and SDK contracts (rough PRD)
content:
SUMMARY:
This is a working PRD sketch for a latency-focused tool adaptor and SDK contract set for Hosted API. The angle: make tool-calling and structured output physically efficient for low-latency client flows (mobile/edge) and medium-latency server flows, with deterministic fallback behavior when full tool orchestration would violate SLOs. This doc is intentionally pragmatic: lightweight wire contracts, an incremental response model, and client ergonomics for graceful degradation.

Context and motivation:
- We ship ever-more complex tool graphs (search, DB lookups, action APIs). In many real apps a single turn must avoid high tail latency.
- Existing drafts focus on streaming semantics and typed outputs; we need a clear contract that prioritizes latency SLOs and provides predictable client behavior when tool calls are slow or unavailable.
- Developers want minimal SDK surface to: (1) opt-in to progressive results, (2) receive structured action frames, (3) control budgeted tool attempts, (4) reconcile partial results on reconnect.

Primary goals (MUST):
- Define a compact incremental-frame protocol for hosted streaming that signals action/tool intents, speculative placeholders, and final resolved actions.
- Standardize an SDK-level API for positive/negative time budgets per call (client can declare usable latency budget).
- Define deterministic fallback semantics (short answer stub, cached result, local heuristic) when a tool call exceeds its budget or fails.
- Ensure structured output schema (JSON-L) can be emitted progressively and validated incrementally by clients.
- Provide observability hooks and telemetry labels to map user-visible latency buckets to internal tool latency and batch decisions.

Secondary goals (SHOULD):
- Provide a mobile-friendly tiny runtime (JS/Swift/Kotlin) pattern (<= 10 KB overhead) for progressive parsing of frames.
- Offer a compatibility layer for current streaming clients: server can emit compact frames even when older SDKs receive full-text chunks.

Non-goals (explicitly out):
- Not a full rework of tool-security model; assume existing auth and verification remain.
- Not introducing a new heavyweight orchestration language—keep the adaptor surface minimal.

Key concepts and vocabulary:
- frame: smallest incremental unit in the stream. Compact, newline-delimited JSON-L (one JSON object per line) that is parseable by streaming parsers.
- action-intent: token emitted by the model indicating it wants to call a tool; includes id, declared cost/budget estimate, and outputs schema.
- action-placeholder: short textual stub or summary the model can emit while the tool runs.
- action-result: final structured output from the tool or a fallback result type.
- budget: client-declared latency allowance for a request (ms) used by routing and decision heuristics.

Wire-level sketch (compact frames):
- frame.type: one of ["text", "intent", "placeholder", "result", "commit", "telemetry"].
- frame.id: string id for correlating intents/results.
- frame.schema: optional short schema id (eg: "user-profile.v2")
- frame.body: string or short JSON depending on type

Example progressive transcript (newline-delimited frames):
{"type":"text","id":"r1","body":"Starting analysis..."}
{"type":"intent","id":"a1","body":"search:query='companies redwood inference'","schema":"search-result.v1"}
{"type":"placeholder","id":"a1","body":"(searching — results will appear)"}
[tool executes, maybe bumped to dedicated capacity]
{"type":"result","id":"a1","body":{"top_hit":"redwood-inference.com","snippet":"developer-first inference platform"},"schema":"search-result.v1"}
{"type":"commit","id":"a1","body":"committed"}

Budgeted invocation semantics (client -> server):
- Client supplies header X-Client-Budget-MS: <int>. Optional: per-action hints in messages.
- Server uses budget to: route to low-latency pools, abbreviate tool calls (cached or approximate), or replace with a placeholder/fallback.
- If tool cannot finish within budget, server emits: frame.type="result" with field fallback_reason set to one of ["budget", "timeout", "capacity"] and a fallback_kind like ["cached", "stub", "approx"].

Deterministic fallback types (examples):
- cached: return last-known stored result (explicitly marked with age_ms).
- stub: short synthesized answer from other model-only path (e.g., low-temp summary) with metric confidence <0.6.
- approx: quick heuristic computation (local index) that approximates true result.

SDK ergonomic proposals (developer-facing):
1) Minimal callback surface: onFrame(frame) { /* receives parsed frames */ } onComplete(summary) onError(err)
2) Declarative call outcomes: let call = client.invoke({ prompt, budget_ms, toolPreference: ['fast','accurate'] }) call.on('frame', f => ...) call.cancel()
3) Local replay reconciliation: SDK persists frames locally in a session log; on reconnect it asks server for commit markers and reconciles placeholders with final results.
4) Small-footprint mobile parser: streaming parser that can handle newline-delimited frames without building a full JSON stream (no DOM). Provide a C-friendly option for embedded runtimes.

Structured output and schema management:
- Use short schema ids (namespace.version) to keep frames compact. Full schema definitions live in model catalog and console.
- Clients may request on-demand schema fetch: header X-Fetch-Schema: true — server will send a telemetry frame with schema URL or base64 schema payload if needed.
- Schema evolution: allow additive changes; clients must tolerate unknown fields and receive a schema-change frame when major version increments.

Observability and metrics (must ship):
- Expose per-request: client_budget_ms, tool_total_ms, tool_attempts, fallback_counter, result_age_ms
- Add histogram for tail latency with breakdown by tool vs model vs network.
- Tag traces with routing decision (fast-path, dedicated, cached-fallback, speculative-local).

Rollout plan (incremental):
- Phase 0 (experiment): implement compact frame emission behind feature flag for small set of internal SDKs; add budget header passthrough and fallback markers. (4–6 weeks)
- Phase 1 (opt-in beta): public SDKs support onFrame callback and budget header; console can show aggregated fallback rates and age. (6–8 weeks)
- Phase 2 (SLA-backed): default fast-path routing for customers with dedicated pools; compatibility layer with older streaming clients. (8–12 weeks)

Success metrics (initial):
- 25% reduction in 99th percentile client-observed latency for tool-heavy routes in beta customers.
- Fallback rate <= 5% for target latency buckets in production after Phase 1 tuning.
- Developer adoption: 30+ internal and external teams using the onFrame API within 3 months of Beta.

Security and safety notes:
- Fallback stubs and cached results must be annotated clearly in frames; clients should never assume fallback == authoritative.
- Schema fetch must respect data residency/consent rules (do not leak schema payloads with PII).

Open questions / tradeoffs (TO RESOLVE):
- How prescriptive should we be about fallback content quality (confidence score thresholds)?
- Should clients be able to request per-action retry budgets distinct from total request budget?
- Level of server-side heuristics: should we expose tuning knobs (aggressiveness) to customers via console?
- Interoperation with existing typed-tool handshakes: can the compact frames map directly to our typed tool contracts, or is a shim needed?

Dependencies / owners:
- Serving-runtime: need low-overhead frame emitter + budget-aware router (owner: Miguel Torres)
